PROSPEROUS AND PROGRESSIVE. 


Sun Life Assurance Co, of Canada. 


HEAD OFFICE, - - MONTREAL. 


A YEAR OF PROSPERITY. 


The year 1893 was, in many respects, the most 
satisfactory which the Sun Life Assurance 
Company of Canada has yet experienced. 

The following summary will show that not only 
is the financial position of the Company eminently 
satisfactory, but that gains of a very substantial 
and gratifying character have been madein every 
department of the business. 

The Income from premiums, interest and rents 
amounted, after deducting re-assurances, to 
$1,240,483.12—or over $4,000 for every working day 
of the year—an increase during the twelve months 
of $105,615.51. An addition of nearly $600,000 has 
been made to the Assets, bringing them up to 
$4,001,776.90. The Company has thus been able to 
add to its accumulations more than fifty-five per 
cent. of the life premiums received during the 
year, a fact which speaks for itself. The Surplus 
also shows asubstantial increase, and now amounts 
to $288,595.65 over all liabilities and capital stock. 
This showing is specially gratifying in view of 
the fact that profits are now divided yearly ona 
large proportion of the Company’s policies, and 
the undistributed surplus cannot, therefore, accu- 
mulate as rapidly as under the old system, when 
everything was reserved until the end of the 
quinquennial term. 

The Assets are in excellent condition. About 
eighty-five per cent. of the investments consist of 
municipal debentures and first mortgages on real 
estate valued at considerably over six million 
dollars. The remainder comprises loans on the 
Company’s own policies, the Company’s head 
office building, and minor items. The real estate 
held as the result of foreclosure is only about two 
per cent. of the entire assets, and even this small 
amount has been decreasing year by year. The 
return received is as satisfactory as the security, 
the rate being 5.88 per cent. on the average real- 
ized assets.

43rp AnnuAL REporT. 


This is the Jubilee Year in the history of the Young Men’s 
Christian Association. That it has been a tree of God’s planting 
there can be no manner of doubt. Its results are for time and 
eternity. It hds been an important factor in breaking down the 
barriers which previously existed between the various branches of 
the Church of Christ. Its educational influence in developing the 
rank and file of the laity has given a wonderful impetus to all forms 
of Christian and philanthropic work in all lands. Its beneficent 
work in “ Prevention,” and also in “‘ Rescue,” upon the lives of the 
many thousands of young men who now crowd into city centres is 
a matter of history. But, perhaps, its best work is seen in that ever 
increasing list of honored men, from all lands, whose lives have 
been touched by its influence, and who have lent their hand and 
heart to the betterment of the world, and the incoming of the 
Kingdom of Christ. 

For the information of our members, we give a brief historical 
review of the Young Men’s Christian Association, believing that 
they will be more than ever interested in its “present” and 
“future ’’ development, and enter more heartily into the work of 
another year because they are acquainted with its romantic past :— 


In the year 1841, George Williams went to London, England, from the town ot 
Bridgewater, and secured a situation as junior assistant in the dry goods establish- 
ment of Hitchcock & Co’y, St. Paul’s Churchyard. Here he found 80 fellow-clerks 
—very few were Christians, and many were profligate. His own conversion had 
occurred just prior to his leaving home, at the age of 16. His anxiety for the 
welfare of his associates led him to gather a small band of Christians in his bedroom 
at the close of the day’s work for prayer and Bible study. They invited their care- 


10 


less associates to join them, and many were converted, so that the room became too 
small. A meeting of all the Christian young men in the house was called for 


JUNE 6, 1844, 


to establish the work on a broader basis. At this meeting it was decided to organize 
the Young Men’s Christian Association, the object being ‘‘to improve the spiritual 
condition of young men engaged in the drapery and other trades.” Twelve young 
men formed the first membership. At the close of the first year there were 160 
members. In 1845, T. H. TARLETON was engaged as the first paid Secretary, and 
after eleven years’ service, he was succeeded by WILLIAM EpDwyn SHIPTON, who 
filled the office of local secretary until 1878, and to his wise administration was 
largely due the development of the work in Great Britain and on the Continent, and 
the establishment of the World’s Conferences. He was succeeded by Wm. HIND 
SMITH, who is the present Secretary at Exeter Hall, and who will welcome the 
delegates at the coming Jubilee Convention. 


Notable amongst the men who helped the Association on its mission in these early 
years we might mention the Rev. J. C. Ryle, afterwards Lord Bishop of Liverpool ; 
Rev. Robert S. Candlish, D.D., afterwards Principal of the New College, Edin- 
burgh ; Rev. Newman Hall, who has recently died; Rev. Wm. Arthur, author of 
“The Tongue of Fire ;”’ Rev. Alexander Duff, D.D.; the Rev. Dean Alford, D.D.; 
Mr. George Hitchcock, and Lord Shaftesbury. 


At the opening of the first building rented by the Association at 165 Aldersgate 
in 1854, Mr. George Hitchcock said: ‘‘I don’t understand detaching my business 
from my religion. [ think my business is my religion. If God has brought these 
young men under my influence as a business man, I believe that to be a talent from 
Him which I am to use for His glory. I feel deep ba ai with this Institution. 
It has hold of my heart ; it has hold of my judgment.” 


In 1846 a deputation from the London Association visited Manchester, Liverpool, 
Taunton and Leeds, and formed the nucleus of an Association in each town. Then 
the work spread into France, Switzerland and Germany. 


On the 19th November, 1851, the pioneer Association in America was organized in 
the basement of the St. Helen Street Baptist Church in this city. The Rev. F. W. 
Marling, now of New York, was the chairman at that meeting, and afterwards became 
the first Secretary of the Association, and we have several on our membership roll 
to-day who were present at that first meeting. The extension of the work on this 
continent dated from the first International Convention, held at Buffalo in 18 54. There 
the International Committee was formed. The holding of these annual Conventions, 
and the supervision of the work on this continent by the Committee, has produced 
marvellous results. The cost of this work of supervision has grown from $1,000 in 
1866 to $89,000 in 1893, and from one secretary to twenty-five paid agents, whose 
entire time is occupied. The Associations have grown from one in 1851, to 1,438 in 

1893, owning a property valued at $14,779,676, and’ with a total membership of 


i 263,616 young men. 


11 


The number of Associations at present in the world :— 


Associations. Membership.

What wonderful strides in a short half century! The earth has been girdled by 
this brotherhood, which ignores color and race. How the ties of a common effort 
have bound together members of different denominations. God’s stamp has been 
manifestly upon it. It has united the young men of the world in a common effort on 
behalf of their fellows. 

Mr. George Williams, who planted this beneficent tree, still lives to witness its 
marvellous growth. He is now the head of the firm which he entered in 1841 as 
a junior. He has given his best efforts to the interests of this work. Tens of 
thousands of young men will revere his name as one of the benefactors of this 
century. 


The Building of the Young Men’s Christian Association, on 
Dominion Square, stands with its doors open to young men from 
8 a.m. to 1o p.m. throughout the entire year. As a matter of fact, 
only eight hours out of the twenty-four are its doors closed. It isa 
practical expression of the interest felt by a great community in the 
YOUNG MEN who live and labor within its limits, and extends its 
beneficent hospitality to those who come as strangers in its midst. 
It is a most valuable adjunct to the business houses and manu- 
factories, and an effective co-worker with the parents of the city. 

In closing another year’s record of the local work, we have to 
acknowledge God’s goodness in many ways. In the harmony that 
has prevailed in conducting so largé and varied a work ; in the 
new men that have been led to dedicate their lives to Christian 
work: in the development of a larger number of volunteer 
workers, and in the many young men who have been led to settle 
the question of their eternal life through faith in the atoning sacrifice 
of Jesus Christ. 

SOME FACTS, 


The average daily attendance of young men who make use of 
the Building has increased from 503 last year to 890. This shows 
the appreciation of the work by the young men of the city. 


12 


During the year more than 800 young men exercised in the 
Gymnasium and made use of the physical privileges. Two hundred 
and twenty-eight religious meetings and Bible Classes for young men 
only have been held, with a total attendance of’ 16,746 young men. 
Its workers have distributed personally amongst the young men in 
the central part of the city 29,000 printed invitations to its rooms 
and meetings. Fifty-seven lectures, entertainments, or gatherings 
of a social character have been held. It has placed 320 young men 
in boarding houses. Four hundred and ninety young men have 
applied for employment. It has helped 87 of these to secure good 
business positions, and aided hundreds of others by counsel and 
advice. 

The number of new members who joined, shows a decrease of 
143. While this was anticipated on account of the novelty of 
the Building at first, still the in-coming committee should not be 
satisfied until the membership reaches 1,500. It can be done by 
faithful work during each month of the year. We are glad to note 
the large number of members who have renewed. 


A GREAT SCHOOL. 


There are but few of our citizens who realize that this Building is 
fast becoming a great educational centre for commercial and 
mechanical young men. This is a coming feature, and one which 
will have a most important bearing upon the permanency of the 
work in securing the sympathy and co-operation of the business 
men, and in leading to its extension in branches in other parts of 
the city. In its classes there were enrolled 324 young men, who, 
instead of wasting their time in idleness after their day’s work, are 
here engaged in laying the foundation for larger usefulness. 
Three educational lecture courses were planned. The Library 
was placed in excellent shape, and a librarian added. To 
secure increased results at present within our reach, the entire 
educational work, including the Library, Reading Room, Classes 
and Lectures, should be placed under one secretary, who would be 
be. responsible for its development. Those who sympathise with 
young men who are anxious to get along in life, will find here a 
splendid channel for their benevolence. 


Oy LE a Oe NE OE od eT Oe LS oe EE Me tae TT 


15 


RELIGIOUS ACTIVITIES. 


The religious work enters into every department. The Young 
Men’s Meetings and Bible Classes only form the rallying point of 
this work. Unusual interest has been manifested in the classes for 
Bible Study, both in the Junicr and Senior Department. This is 
full of encouragement, as the needs of this time are men who are 
well grounded in a knowledge of the Scriptures. The aim of the 
Association is to develop members who will not only feel a 
personal interest and responsibility for the spiritual welfare of 
young men, but who will become aggressive centres for such 
work in their business and social life, as well as at the Building. 
We are glad to report a great advance in this direction. But 
much more remains to be done. If every active member mani- 
fested an interest in the spiritual welfare of his companions in 
business, what a mighty result would be obtained in this in-coming 
year. Remember, that was the seed thought that gave us the Asso- 
ciation! Let the eternal welfare of the young men who are 
‘ndifferent to these things and who are drifting carelessly to des- 
truction, arouse us all to a sense of our responsibility and our great 
opportunity. 

It is a pleasure to report that the Building is being increasingly 
used by men who, seeing their need, are led to seek spiritual counsel 
and help. Many of these are now working with us, and walking in 
the power of the renewed life. 

The Victoria Square Building has been sold to Mr. J. D. Davis 
for $53,000. 

MEN WHO GO OUT. 


We have to thank God for the ever-increasing list of men who 
have gone out from our membership into active work. ‘This year 
has been no exception. D. W. CorsettT left in June to take the 
work in Honolulu and the Hawaiian Islands; ARTHUR F. BELL 
went to the Training School, at Springfield, in December, prepar- 
atory to accepting the Secretaryship at Halifax, N.S., in July, 1894 ; 
P. C. Lesiiz, after acting as Secretary of the McGill College 
Association last session, has gone to the International Office, New 
York, to assist (temporarily) in the College Department, and, on 
completion of his medical course, will enter the young men’s work 


14 


on the foreign field; Mr. T. Duncan PATTON, for six years 
associated in the work here, has accepted the Secretaryship of the 
Winnipeg Association, and will enter upon his duties July rst ; and 
Mr. C. B. PowrTer will enter the Training School, at Springfield, 
in September, preparatory to taking a position as Physical Director. 
This is a large contribution, and while it weakens us for the 
present, we believe “there is that that scattereth and yet increaseth, 
and we look for other workers eager to fill these vacancies. “ Pray 
ye the Lord of the harvest that He would thrust out other laborers 
into the harvest-field.” 

We were honored by a visit from His Excellency the Governor- 
General of Canada and Lady Aberdeen, who accepted a reception 
tendered to them by the Board of Directors. Lord Aberdeen’s 
intimate knowledge of the Association work in Great Britain, and 
his expressions of full sympathy with the work here, and his surprise 
at the complete equipment and appointments of this Building, made 
his visit one which our Directors and members wil] not soon forget. 


FOR THE FUTURE. 


What are our needs? The Directors are face to face with large 
opportunities. This Building, so useful in reaching and influencing 
the lives of thousands of men, cannot cover the City.” “Pornr SP, 
CHARLES, with its crowds of young men, needs a similar work. 
Livery year delayed sees the lives of hundreds of young men not reached, 

ho otherwise might be saved; This is a great responsibility. 

The Dominion Square Building should have $25,000 removed 
from its indebtedness. This would give the Directors a surplus 
income which would enable them to supervise the work, when 
established, at another point. When munificent gifts are now 
coming so freely from citizens, and Montreal is honoring herself 
thereby, will not some friend consider this work, and take advantage 
of this grand opportunity for a profitable investment. The shaping 
of the lives of young men between the ages of 18 and 30 has the 
immediate future destiny of the City and nation in its grasp. Who 
will start the list ? 

A larger band of VOLUNTEER WoRKERS from the active member- 
ship. This must be the aim for this year. The work demands it. 
_ The results could be doubled. The increase of paid officials is a 


15 


dangerous policy. ‘The true spirit of the Association is the develop- 
ment of a large VOLUNTEER FORCE from the membership, where 
every man is given his separate work, and held responsible for it. 
This is a guarantee for the future. Who will come forward ? How- 
ever busy you are, surely you can find some moments to give to 
some definite part of the work. Let us hear from you? 

Let each member make this work a subject of daily prayer. No 
co-operation can be as effective as this. Plead God’s promises for 
the salvation of young men. Ask in faith, nothing doubting. Look 
earnestly for the answer, and the 44th year in the history of this 
Association will be indelibly engraved on the lives of hundreds of 
young men. 


Secretary.

FINANCE COMMITTEE. 


Accompanying this Report are the Financial Statements of the Association for the 
year ending 30th April, 1894, duly audited by Messrs. P. S. Ross & Sons. These 
contain the gratifying information that the revenue of the Association for the fiscal 
year has balanced its expenditure, leaving a small sum to the good. This result has 
only been attained by the generous assistance of the members and of the Board. The 
effort lately made by the young men (enthusiastically assisted by many of the boys of 
the Junior Department) procured $606.14, in addition to $156 of new memberships. 
This left a prospectiye deficit of a little over $500, which, at a meeting of the Board 
held last Friday evening, was there and then guaranteed and subseribed, enabling 
the Association to close without debt, with every outstanding account paid off. 

Most welcome and valued aid has been received from some of the younger members 
of the Committee. 

As an illustration of the earnest work performed in connection with the finances, it 
may be stated that our subscribers numbered last year about 600, each one of whom 
has to be visited. Many of the subscribers of 1892-93 considered their contributions 
(of 1892-93) as ‘‘ special,” and not to be repeated ; besides which, owing to business 
depression, some heretofore supporters felt obliged to withdraw or decrease their 
subscriptions. To make good these losses, and to keep income from this source 
abreast of last year (which the Committee have managed to do), new names had to 
be obtained. From 125 of such new names, about $750 of new revenue was thus 
obtained. 

It goes without saying that the work of the Financial Secretary, Mr. T. D. Patton, 
for the past difficult year, has been no light one. He has received efficient aid from 
Mr. Percy H. Cushing. The Association cannot be too grateful for the onerous 
work thus done by the staff in addition to their secretarial duties. A change, looking 
for the relief of the Secretaries from the excessive burden of this office work, will be 
brought about for the coming year. 

The estimates for the coming year will show a deficit of $1,250. If 250 of our 
members could each undertake to procure at least one new member during the year, 
an even balance would be assured, thereby removing the strain on the Finance Com- 
mittee, who anticipate a difficult year ahead of them in 1894-95. A statement is 
attached, showing that each member for his $5.00 ticket receives what has cost the 


Association close upon $20.00. 
D. |W. ‘ROSS, 


Chairman Finance Committee.

MEMBERSHIP. 


On this the second full year of our occupancy of the building, it was thought by 
the Directors that our membership would be considerably less on account of the loss 
of many who joined because it was a new thing. This has been true in some 
measure, as will be seen by the large number of members (479) who have not 
renewed. But the new members added has made the cash receipts $5,651,—$351 in 
excess of last year. The membership roll should reach 1,500. The capacity of the 
building is sufficient to handle that number, and we hope the new Committee will 
aim at that mark. The number of new members secured was 494 senior and 136 
junior. The following statement will be of interest, as showing the occupations of 
the members, and also their church relations :—

LIBRARY REPORT. 


Your Committee have great pleasure in reporting that, through the timely aid of 
generous friends, large and varied additions have been made during the year to the 
Library; and, through the invaluable services of our Librarian, Miss Charlton, the 
books have been rearranged, catalogued, kept in the best order, widely and wisely 
distributed among the reading membership. For the better protection of the books, 
and for fixing responsibility, the Library-room has been enclosed, but in such a manner 
as, at the same time, to enable the Librarian to have complete oversight of the 
Reading-room. It is a pleasure to notice that the standard of reading is being raised, 
as many who were content formerly with juvenile fiction are now seeking for the best 
books in history and literature and the iatest books in experimental science. Much, 
however, remains to be done in this direction. The planning of courses of reading 
for next winter should receive the early consideration of the incoming Committee. 
Your Committee gratefully recognizes the wise and princely gifts of the late Mr. 
Redpath to the students of McGill, and hopes that Christian friends will not forget 
the needs of the hundreds of young men debarred from the University, and whose 
reading matter is obtained solely from our library shelves. Of the 3,000 books now 
in the Senior Library :—580 are works of reference ; 410, religious and devotional ; 
406, fiction , 315, history; 268, biography; 227, poetry and general literature ; 288, 
science and art; 198, magazines ; 225, travels; 110, political and social. Books 
added during the year number 285, the circulation since last September 5,650.

YOUNG MEN’S MEETING. 


This meeting still holds its prominent place in the work of the Association, and 
we believe the spiritual pulse of the whole work can be felt here. 

We commenced the year with bright prospects and looked forward to greater 
success in attendance and results than had been accomplished before. Although we 
have fallen short of our ideal, advance has been made. ‘The attendance was about 
4,035, an average of 77,—an increase over the previous year. 

The results in the spiritual life cannot be numbered, but we know that scarcely a 
Saturday night has passed without from one to half a dozen manifesting a desire 
to lead a Christian life, and many have found Christ as a personal Saviour, as their 
testimonies bear witness, and others have been strengthened in their Christian life. 
We have tried to meet the need of all classes attending the meeting, therefore one 
quarter’s topics were composed of some of the more difficult portions of God’s Word, 
and were handled by very able speakers, and proved of great interest. We have 
been especially pleased to see the leaders of the gymnasium classes attending from 


29 


time to time. This cannot but have good effect on the rest of the members of the 
physical department. As this meeting is especially for our members, we believe some 
organized efiort should be put forth to get the members of this department to attend. 
We are convinced if our active members were faithful in attending at least some of 
these meetings, we would have no trouble in getting others to do so. We must first 
be faithfnl ourselves if we would win others. 

We would like to thank our friends who have so faithfully presided at the piano 
and organ, and led the singing, Messrs. H. Griffiths, Thomas Somers and G. H. Porteous. 

In closing this report, we wish to make a personal appeal to our members to 
support this meeting during the coming year, as it is thoroughly a young men’s 
meeting. Shall we not, as a thank-offering to God for all the blessings of the past 
year, say : I will have some part in this matter, and, God helping me, I will do what 


I can to make it a blessing to others. 
J. WILSON, 


Chairman. 


MEN’S MEETING. 


With an attendance varying from 60 to 400 the men’s meeting has been held 
regularly throughout the year. Whenever possible, we have secured any prominent 
visitors in the City to address the meeting. 

While our object has been to reach the throngs of young men who are to be found 
on St. Catherine Street, and in the boarding houses Sunday afternoons, we have not 
fully succeeded. A new attraction will shortly be added in the form of an orchestra, 
which Mr, J. H. Ferns has agreed to secure. Our Building should be a rallying 
point Sunday at 4.15, and we hope that the new committee will make it such. The 
McGill College Association has asked. that we co-operate with them during next 
winter in securing three or four speakers from other Cities. With these and the able 
speakers in the City there is no reason why Association Hall could not be filled every 
week. Shall we not look forward to this and use our endeavours to bring it about ? 


WALTER E. CUSHING, 
Secretary. 


YOUNG MEN’S BIBLE CLASS. 


Your Committee beg to report as follows :-—The attendance at this class during 
the past year has been very good, being 3,595, an average of 71. This average 
would have been materially increased but for the fact of other Gospel meetings 
being held at the same time as the class on several occasions, as on Sunday, July 9th, 
the meetings of the Christian Endeavor Convention brought our attendance down to 
30, the smallest since being in the present building, and on February 25th, no class 
was held so as to enable the members to attend the last afternoon meeting conducted 
by Rev. B. Fay Mills. Since this date the numbers have steadily increased ; the 
average of the last six Sundays being 100. 


30 


Our Study during the past year has been ‘‘ The Life of Christ” in the four 
Gospels, followed bya course in the ‘‘ Acts.” On March Ist we began a course of 
lessons entitled “ From the Brickfields of Egypt to Mount Pisgah.” 

The attendance and interest of late seem to show that the practical manner in 
which the lessons are applied, especially as they bear on the needs of young men, are 
greatly appreciated by the members of the class, particularly those who are just 
starting the in Christian life. i 

Through the benevolent fund of the class we have had the privilege of being of 
assistance to several of our members who have been sick. 

During the past year we have had the pleasure of listening to Dr. Grenfell of the 
‘¢ Deep Sea Mission,’ Messrs. Stark and Jarrett, Missionaries on their way to Peru, 
John Currie of Glasgow, and Mr. S. Kimura of Japan, and we are indebted to Rev. 
E. Scott, and Messrs. D. W. Ross and C. T. Williams, who so ably conducted the 
class in the absence of Mr. Budge. The thanks of the class are also due Mr. W. T. 
Walmsley and others who have kindly looked after the music and singing. 


LEWIS A. WINTER, 
Chatrman. 


INVITATION. 


If some of the younger Christians only knew how much strength comes from 
serving on this Committee, there would not be as many unoccupied ‘‘ corners ”’ on 
Saturday evening. Though there may appear to be some trials connected with this 
part of the vineyard, they are lost to sight as we busy ourselves inviting men to the 
gospel meetings. No branch of the work comes as much into contact with unreached 
young men as this. Sixteen workers have distributed 29,400 invitations during the 
year. The little slip, handed out on the street is often supplemented with a kindly 
smile or a word of invitation, and while it is not possible to know the full results, we 
are confident that the bread cast upon the waters will return after many days. Nor 
are we without visible results, for quite often young men are brought to the meetings 
for the first time. 

Two difficulties have faced us during the year: Ist, Sickness and business have 
reduced the number of workers ; 2nd, Strict economy has been necessary in our 
printing, limiting the attractiveness of the cards and dodgers. We would like to 
suggest that some gentleman form an endowment fund for the tract and invitation 
work. This would meet the latter need, and no doubt such encouragement would 
induce more active members to add their efforts to this work. 

Owing to nearly all workers being engaged in Sunday-school, at 3.30 Sunday 
afternoon, work in connection with the Men’s Meeting has been for the present 
discontinued. 


With sincere thanks to our Master for the privilege of working in this corner 


of His vineyard, we respectfully submit this report. 
GEO. COMRIE, 
Chairman. 


ol 


EXTENSION FUND. 


The extension fund was organized in 1889 with a double object in view : Ist, to 
develop systematic giving ; 2nd, to assist in extending this work for and by young” 
men beyond the borders of our own City. 


NEED.—The Home and Foreign work constitute our field. 


I. Foreign mission lands with 200,000,000 young men have less than a dozen 
men giving their whole time to Y.M.C.A. work, while Canada and the United States, 
with only 13,000,000, have over 1,400. India’s 50,000,000 young men have less 
than 6 giving their whole time in the interests of this work, while Canada’s 1,000,000 
are provided with over 78. In 1889 the International Convention instructed the 
International Committee to raise money and’send Mr. J. Trumball Swift to Japan, as 
its representative. Since then Mr. David McConaughy has gone to Madras, Mr. R. 
S. Miller to Tokyo, Mr. Myron A. Clark to Brazil, and during the past year Mr. J. 
Campbell White went to Calcutta, his first year’s expenses being supplied by a 
member of the Montreal Association. These have gone forth to establish Associations, 
which will be illustrations, and to train native young men to carry forward the work. 
Urgent appeals have been sent by at least 250 Missionaries asking that Associations 
be established in China, Ceylon, Turkey and Asia Minor. India is called ‘‘ The 
Rudder of Asia.’? Thus far the funds from Montreal have been devoted to the 
support of Mr. McConaughy, but will in the future go to Mr. White. How much 
shall the amount be ? 


2. Th Home Field is divided as follows: (a) The Provincial Committee with 
headquarters in Toronto has only one man surpervising the work of twenty-nine 
Associations in Ontario and Quebec. On him largely rests the duty of securing 
secretaries for the different places, assisting Associations when in difficulties, and 
giving counsel wherever and whenever needed. ‘They require more funds. (4) The 
International Committee has for its field the whole Continent and those foreign lands 
where they have representatives. Besides the foreign work, they foster and establish 
special work for German, French, Indian, Colored, Railroad and College young men. 
To their watchful supervision is due the advancement of the work in America. They 
look to every Association for help. (c) The Young Men’s Christian Association Train- 
ing School at Springfield, where I out of 10 Secretaries, and 4 out of 10 Physical 
Directors on this Continent, have been trained. This School has no endowment. 


Ways AND MEANS.—Fifty-seven members give systematically each week or 
month. Three give $25 each per year, and one gives $100. To the weekly and 
monthly contributors we look for sympathy and support. Will you not enlist more 
in this advance movement ? 

The departure of Mr. D. W. Corbett, who was the main-stay of this work, and the 
resignation of Mr. W. J. Wright, who had served for over two years as its efficient 
and faithful Secretary, had a demoralizing effect, and it was not until the visit of Mr. 
L. D. Wishard, in January, that a new fire was enkindled. We pray ‘* Thy kingdom 
come,” and we labor to the end that all nations may soon hear the ‘‘ glad tidings.”

EDUCATIONAL COMMITTEE. 


The Educational work of the Association continues to occupy an important place 
(The manner in which the members respond to the 
privileges offered by the Educational Committee, proves that this aur’ of our 
work meets an important need among our young men.) ) 

Indeed, it would be impossible to overestimate the importance of cise: evening 
classes to over 300 young, who were in attendance during the past winter. 


in the year’s programme. 


Without 


Va 


DO 


neglecting the educational effect of the work it has been the aim of the Committee to 
arrange the subjects of the course so as to make them of practical value in the 
everyday life of young men. 

The regular work has accordingly been organized in eight different classes, viz. : 
French, (Elementary and Advanced), Shorthand, Commercial Arithmetic, Book- 
Keeping, Penmanship, Mechanical Drawing, Vocal Music, and a Chautauqua Class. 
Subjects which have their educational value, and at the same time form a young 
man’s stock in trade for a business life. 

As the work of these evening classes presents many difficulties, the Committee felt 
it to be their duty to secure for the management of these classes, men whose teaching 
power and scholarship were of ‘the first order. The Committee have been very 
fortunate in securing a staff of gentlemen for this work, which, in point of teaching 
power and knowledge of their respective subjects, compares favorably with the staff 
of any of our secondary schools. 

There could be only one result from this combination of circumstances—the classes 
were interested and orderly. The work was carried on in a regular and systematic 
manner from the beginning to the close of the coursg, and the results were all that 
could be expected under the circumstances. 

In addition to the regular course two special courses were provided, one upon legal 
points and the second upon medical subjects, both bearing upon the requirements of 
everyday life. These lectures were delivered by the members of the legal and 
medical profession of the City, and they were well attended. The influence of these 
regular and special courses upon the young men in attendance, from every point of 
view, must be such as to commend this department of work to the friends of the 
Association. 

After careful consideration of the finances, the Executive Committee was able to 
appropriate only $350.00 for the educational work last year. The amount is quite 
inadequate. In order to plan the work on a satisfactory basis, and to meet the 
reasonable requests of our young men, at least twice the amount should be at the 
disposal of the Educational Committee. 

As this amount cannot reasonably be taken from the ordinary funds of the 
Association the Committee confidently appeals to the friends of the Association for 
special assistance in this department. 

In order to organize all the educational work of the Association upon a more 
satisfactory basis, it has been decided to unite the Educational work ; the library 
and the reading room in a distinct department, and to place this department under 
the supervision of a special officer. This arrangement, which will come into force in 
September next, will greatly facilitate the work of the Committee, in the general 
management and supervision of the educational classes. The Committee look 
forward to increased efficiency and interest in this department, under the new 
arrangement.

SOCIAL COMMITTEE. 


Your Committee presented the following programme for the year ending 30th 
April, 1894. 

Six Stereopticon Entertainments, by Mr. Hugh Russell. 

Four Evenings in Natural History with Mr. C. T. Williams, illustrated with 
' stereopticon. 

OcToBER 5TH.—Address by Mr. Chas. T. Williams, “ Ethics of Business Life.” 

NOVEMBER 2ND.—A night with the Harmony Male Quartette. 

* I4TH AND 16TH.—J. E. Budgett Meakin, Illustrated Lectures on 

Morocco, etc. 

NOVEMBER 30TH.—Musical Evening, under the direction of Mr. Horace W. 
Reyner, A.R.C.O. 

DECEMBER 14TH.—Adadress by S. P. Leet, B.C.L., “Law Points for Young Men.” 

JANUARY IsT.—New Year’s Reception to Members and Friends. 

a 18tH.—Address by Mr. George Hague, ‘‘ Labor and Capital.” 

MARCH 15TH.—Address by Mr. Herbert B. Ames, ‘‘ Canada as a Young Man’s 
Home.” 

APRIL 17TH. —Reception to Young Men’s Bible Classes of the City Sunday Schools. 
Addresses by Sir William Dawson, Mr. Fred Meyers and Mr. D. A. Budge. 

The attendance in many cases was not as large as anticipated, and it is a matter 
of regret that more of our members did not avail themselves of the opportunity of 
attending these social gatherings. 


35 


The sincere thanks of the Committee are due and are hereby tendered to the ladies 
of Erskine, Douglas, Crescent Street and Mountain Street Churches for their valuable 
aid. 

We would also convey our thanks to all those who contributed to the success of 
the entertainments. 

Respectfully submitted, 
WM, EEES, 
Chairman. 


RECEPTION COMMITTEE. 


More has been attempted by the Reception Committee this year than ever before. 
Besides having one or more members on duty at the Building each evening to 
receive and welcome strangers four Receptions were planned. Two of these were 
necessarily cancelled, but the Matéonal Reception and the Dry Goods Reception were 
successfully carried out. Hallowe’en was observed with a Mrestde Talk and on 
another evening freshly popped corn was supplied to all comers. More in this line 
could be carried on to advantage. This Committee furnished ushers for the Anniver- 
sary, decorated the Building for New Years and assisted at all social evenings. 

The attendance of members for evening duty was well sustained until February, 
since which time, however, fewer of the workers have kept their appointments, though 
the faithfulness of some is worthy of the highest commendation. 

The throngs of young men frequenting the Building every evening make a larger 
force of efficient workmen a real necessity. Any who would like to assist should 
leave their names with the General Secretary. 

A record was kept 233 evenings, showing 359 workers on duty and 765 visitors 
shown through the Building. The Rooms were closed with a prayer service 101 


evenings with an average attendance of 6. 
R. HENDERSON, 


Chairman 


PHYSICAL DEPARTMENT. 


We are glad to report that the year just closed has been the most successful in the 
history of this Department. Our members have kept up their interest and enthu- 
siasm, and we are pleased to record a marked improvement in every feature of the 
work. 

The Gymnasium and Baths have been open every week day during the year from 8 
a.m.to 10 p.m. During June, July and August, the baths have been open at 6.30 a.m. 
The water supply in the large bath has given every. satisfaction, and the apparatus in 
the Gymnasium is in good order. : 

_The Class averages are as follows: Ist Class, 9 ; 2nd Class, 16 ; 3rd Class, 25 ; 
Preparatory, 38; Boys’, 49; Business Men, 19; Students’, 17 ; Working Boys’, 13 ; 


36 


Pastors’, 9. Each class meets twice a week, except the Boys’, which meets three 
times. The above figures give the average at each session. The attendance during 
the third week of November was 614. Average weekly class attendance for the year, 
450, and the estimated monthly attendance in Gymnasium and Baths, 3,175.

Number of lockers, 862; number in use 30th April, 782. 

There were five confidential talks given on the floor of the Gymnasium by our 
Physical Director. 

The Gymnastic Competition Medals referred to in last year’s Report were awarded 
as follows: The 1st Grade to Arthur J. Lee, 91 per cent. ; and Alex. Murray, jr., 
87 per. cent. The 2nd Grade to W. E. Dixon, 81 per. cent; and B. Wilson, 80 per 
cent. 

During the visit of Their Excellencies, the Governor-General and Lady Aberdeen, 
an exhibition was given in the Gymnasium. Our Physical Director, Mr. W. H. 
all was warmly congratulated by Their Excellencies on the fine appearance of the 
men and the proficiency of the exercises. 

Exhibitions were also given on New Year's day in the building, on the occasion of 
the opening of O’Brien Hall, Point St. Charles, and by the boys at Welcome Hall. 

Basket Bali has maintained its popularity and furnished much enjoyment to both 
members and friends. Several matches with outside teams were played, including 
two games with a team from Burlington, Vt., Y.M.C.A. Eight teams were formed, 
and a tournament of fifty games were played, resulting in a victory for the Veterans, 
who were not defeated in a single match. 

The Bowling Alleys have been used more than ever before. Weekly competitions 
have been carried on throughout the entire season, the highest score made up to date, 
244, by A. R. Forrester. ‘Team competitions are now under way. 

A Course of six Medical Lectures was arranged by the Educational Committee 
especially for the members of this Department, and was well attended. 


OUTDOOR WORK. 


Your Committee secured the use of the Shamrock Grounds three mornings a week 
during the summer season, which was very much appreciated, as shown by the large 
turn outs at the morning practices. 

The interest manifested on the part of our members in outdoor athletics impresses 
your Committee more strongly than ever with our need of a suitable field for athletic 
sports. 


37 


Under this head the Association has carried on a Lacrosse Club with 75 members, 
but we were unable to play matches through lack of grounds. 

Rugby Football had a membership of 58. We had a strong team, but were able 
to arrange only one match, as it was impossible to secure a suitable place to play. 

The Snowshoe Club is one of the most popular of our outdoor sports, having a 
membership of 98, with regular weekly tramps. The athletic events under their 
auspices were the first held, and much interest was displayed. Their season wound 
up with an ‘‘ At Home,” which was one of the most pleasant social events of the 
year. 

A Bicycle Club has been recently organized, with a membership of 25, and gives 
promise of becoming a popular feature of our work. 

There has been a strong desire by many members of our Association for Football, 
Baseball and Tennis, but we have so far been unable to meet the demand. 

For the coming season there is a favorable outlook for athletic grounds, but we 
regret that the season has so far advanced without our being able to definitely state 
plans for the coming year. We hope to be able within a few days to report satis- 
factory arrangements. 

' Mr. Chas. B. Powter, who was appointed Assistant Physical Director in Novem- 
ber, 1892, has resigned to take the Physical Course in the Y.M.C.A. Training 
School at Springfield, Mass. We trust that the experience acquired in our Asso- 
ciation, and the benefit he will derive from his Course of Study, will enable him 
to do excellent service. Mr. O. M. Sharp, one of our leaders, left us early in the 
fall to take charge of the Physical Department in Stanstead College. 

We are pleased to note that Mr. Sidney A. Hall, a member of our first leader’s 
class, has accepted the position of Physical Director of the West End Branch, 
Toronto. 

The valuable services rendered by the leaders is greatly appreciated by your 


Committee. 
ABNER KINGMAN, 


Chatrman. 


EMPLOYMENT. 


Owing to the financial depression during the past year comparatively little was 
accomplished which can be recorded by figures. While only 70 of the 490 applicants 
at this Bureau were directly assisted in securing positions, all deserving cases were 
enquired into and advice given. 


JUNIOR DEPARTMENT. 


In presenting this report we feel that any success achieved has been by our depen- 
dence upon God, who has heard the earnest prayer made by the Executive Committee 
and workers, and from many of the Christian boys, 

The departure of Mr. D. W. CoRBETT in June, 1893, left this work in great need, 
and we feared the result, but Mr. P. H. CUSHING was secured as his successor, and 


38 


has done excellent work, and encouraging results have been obtained on all the lines. 
There has been marked development in committee work,—the members accepting 
the responsibility placed upon them, and doing their work faithfully. The training 
classes for workers have never been so well attended. Four regular and three for 
young converts have been maintained. We feel that many of the future Christian 
workers of the City are being developed in these classes. The interest in Bible Study 
has increased—122 members are members of the Scripture Union, and are regularly 
reading stated portions of God’s word. 

Forty-nine gospel meetings have been held with an average attendance of §5. The 
total number of enquirers whose names and addresses we have is 123, and from the 
change in the lives of 31 we cannot but believe that they have been surrendered to God. 
Twenty-one of our Associate members have united with the Church during the year. 
The Friday night meeting has been the centre of the work, and every effort has been 
-made to make it bright, interesting and attractive. 

Six committees have had the work in charge, with 54 workers, and these are 
gaining valuable experience for their future career. 

The total membership is 230, including 136 new members who joined during the 
year. 

Four socials and entertainments were held which proved valuable in retaining the 
interest of the members, as well as giving them genuine enjoyment. 

The Physical Classes have been well attended—eighty-six day classes for school 
boys, with an average attendance of 49; sixty evening classes for boys employed 
during the day, with an average attendance of 13. The latter class shows the best 
average attendance in the Gymnasium, and we appeal for greater privileges for this 
class another season. The excellent results secured in the Gymnasium work is 
largely due to the faithful work of Mr. Powter, Assistant Instructor. Foot-ball and 
Snowshoe Clubs, and two Basket Ball Tournaments have proved of great interest. 

The mistakes of the year have shown us where we are weak, and how we may 
strengthen its work next year. An encouraging feature has been the harmony that 
has prevailed, not only amongst the Committee, but throughout the whole Depart- 
ment. 

The Library has had 222 readers, with a circulation of 2,736. This is doing a 
good work in storing the boys’ minds with healthy and pure knowledge. 

Representatives from the Department attended the International and Provincial 
Conventions—Messrs. P. H. Cushing, R. C. Patterson, and R. L. Charlton, and 
received much benefit. 

We cannot close without acknowledging the service rendered by Mr. P. H. 
Cushing. It has been by his effort, plan and organization, with God’s blessing, that 
the work has been so faithfully carried out. .

WORK OUTSIDE THE BUILDING. 


HOsPITAL AND VISITATION OF THE SiICK.—Every Sunday morning, 9.30 to 
10.30, a service is held at the General Hospital, to which the convalescent patients 
are invited. This has brought comfort and good cheer to hundreds of invalids who 
have been lonely and discouraged. Mr. Harry Griffiths has rendered faithful service 
by personal attendance, and in notifying the workers. Young men who are sick in: 
boarding-houses or at home, are visited by the members, and whenever their names 
are known by us, watchers at night are provided in cases of serious illness. Our 
members could aid us by promptly reporting at the office any cases of sickness which 
they may know about. 

TRACT WORK AMONGST THE SAILORS. Sou William Law has been the faithful 
centre of this work during the summer months, and, assisted by a number of 
members, they have visited the ships in port, distributing tracts and invitations, and 
co-operating with the Sailors’ Institute in the work. 

MILITARY CAMP.—The Association placed a tent with full equipment for reading- 
room, library, games, etc., in the grounds at Laprarie in June last. Mr. T. Duncan 
Patton had charge, and conducted evangelistic meetings every night amongst the 
men. He was assisted by members from the city. The influence of this work for 
many years has been most beneficial upon the whole character of the camp life, and 
many men date their conversion from these services. , 


POPULAR BECAUSE RELIABLE.
